content: Zinc deficiency is commonly observed in children with kwashiorkor, and their skin lesions typically improve rapidly with zinc supplementation. For raw skin areas, apply a barrier cream such as zinc and castor oil ointment, petroleum jelly, or tulle gras. For skin sores, use gentian violet or nystatin cream. For persistent diarrhea, examine stool samples microscopically if possible. If giardiasis is suspected but stool microscopy cannot be performed, treat with metronidazole at a dose of 5 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7 days. Lactose intolerance is rarely the cause of diarrhea. It should only be diagnosed if watery diarrhea occurs immediately after milk-based feeds and resolves when milk intake is reduced or stopped. Starter F-75 is a low-lactose feed. In exceptional cases, replace milk feeds with yogurt or lactose-free infant formula, and gradually reintroduce milk feeds during the rehabilitation phase. Osmotic diarrhea may be suspected if diarrhea worsens significantly with hyperosmolar F-75 and resolves when the sugar content and osmolarity are reduced. In such cases, use cereal-based starter F-75 or an isotonic commercially available starter F-75. Gradually introduce catch-up F-100 or ready-to-use therapeutic food. If tuberculosis (TB) is strongly suspected, perform a Mantoux test (noting that false-negative results are common) and, if possible, take a chest X-ray. Children admitted to the hospital with complicated severe acute malnutrition can be transferred to outpatient care during the rehabilitation phase. This decision should not be based solely on achieving specific anthropometric or weight-for-height/length outcomes. Children should be discharged to outpatient or community nutritional programs when they have completed parenteral antibiotic treatment, are clinically well and alert, have resolved medical complications, have regained appetite and are eating well, and have reduced or resolved edema. Parents should be prepared for outpatient treatment and encouraged to bring the child back weekly for therapeutic food, vaccinations, and routine vitamin A supplements. Children with severe acute malnutrition should only be discharged from nutritional treatment programs when their weight-for-height/length is at least ≥ -2 z-score and they have had no edema for at least 2 weeks, or their mid-upper-arm circumference is ≥ 125 mm with no edema for at least 2 weeks. The same anthropometric indicator used at admission should be used to confirm recovery. Children admitted with bilateral pitting edema should be discharged based on the indicator routinely used in the national nutrition program. Children should be fed at least five times a day with foods containing approximately 100 kcal and 2–3 g of protein per 100 g of food. Frequent meals with high energy and protein content are essential. Mothers should be counseled on appropriate feeding practices, including providing meals at least five times daily, assisting and encouraging the child to complete meals, and breastfeeding as often as the child desires. Food should be given separately to monitor the child’s intake. After discharge to outpatient care, a follow-up plan should be established to monitor the child until full recovery. Weekly weight checks are recommended. If the child fails to gain weight over a 2-week period, loses weight, or develops loss of appetite or edema, they should be referred back to the hospital for further assessment. Periodic monitoring after discharge is essential to prevent relapse. A mortality audit should be conducted, maintaining a register of admissions, discharges, and deaths, including details such as weight, age, sex, and dates of admission and discharge or death. This helps identify factors that can improve care. For deaths within 24 hours, consider untreated or delayed treatment of hypoglycemia, hypothermia, septicemia, severe anemia, or incorrect rehydration. For deaths within 72 hours, evaluate whether feeding volumes during refeeding were too high or if the formula was incorrect. At night, consider hypothermia due to insufficient covering or lack of night feeds. Weight gain during rehabilitation should be standardized and monitored. Scales should be calibrated daily, and children should be weighed at the same time each day after removing clothing (avoiding hypothermia). Weight gain is categorized as poor (<5 g/kg/day), moderate (5–10 g/kg/day), or good (>10 g/kg/day). If weight gain is poor, assess whether this is a widespread issue requiring a review of case management or specific to individual cases needing reassessment. Check for inadequate feeding, including whether night feeds are given, target energy and protein intakes are achieved, and feeding techniques are appropriate. Evaluate the quality of care, feed preparation, and whether complementary foods are energy-dense enough. If feeding is adequate and there is no malabsorption, suspect hidden infections such as urinary tract infections, otitis media, TB, or giardiasis. Re-examine the child, repeat urine microscopy for white blood cells, examine stools, and, if possible, take a chest X-ray. Consider treatment even in the absence of a confirmatory diagnosis. Children with HIV/AIDS can recover from malnutrition, but recovery may take longer, and treatment failures are more common. Initial nutritional treatment for severe acute malnutrition in children with HIV/AIDS should follow the same protocol as for HIV-negative children. Early diagnosis and correct management, along with routine vaccinations and improved nutrition, are critical to saving lives. Children with HIV are at greater risk for infections such as staphylococcal and pneumococcal infections and TB. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is essential for HIV-infected children. All infants and children should have their HIV status established at their first contact with the health system, ideally at birth or as soon as possible thereafter. HIV testing should be voluntary, with informed consent obtained before testing. In countries with generalized HIV epidemics, all children with unknown HIV status should be offered counseling and testing. Diagnosis of HIV in perinatally exposed infants under 18 months is challenging due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Virological testing is the most reliable method for diagnosing HIV in children under 18 months. For breastfeeding infants, a negative virological test should be repeated 6 weeks after breastfeeding cessation to confirm the absence of HIV infection. Clinical staging of HIV infection helps determine the degree of immune system damage and plan treatment. ART should be initiated immediately for all HIV-infected infants under 60 months, regardless of clinical or immunological status. Triple-drug therapy is the standard of care, with first-line regimens based on two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus one non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) or protease inhibitor. Fixed-dose combinations are preferred for better adherence and reduced cost. Drug dosages must be adjusted as the child grows to avoid under-dosage and resistance development.
